rationale: The FAQ defines pending as accepted but incomplete; the policy independently limits eligibility to a visibly processing transfer. Failed and declined FAQs describe different terminal states.
The runbook explicitly checks pending with no failure, refusal, or completion; the FAQ and policy state the same boundary. Failed/declined runbooks do not establish a pending state.

Both the active policy and runbook independently state the two-business-day window and post-window review action; the FAQ supplies the same window and duplicate-prevention boundary. Requiring both preselected gold IDs is unnecessary.

Three pending sections prohibit a duplicate while processing. The failed-transfer retry rule also directly supplies the decisive boundary: retry is allowed only after terminal failure, so its hard-negative role is incorrect.

The FAQ defines terminal processing failure, the policy limits failure eligibility, and the runbook confirms explicit failed state after submission. The original mapping omitted the runbook's direct support.

The failed runbook says not to reinterpret refusal as failure; both FAQs explicitly contrast technical failure after submission with refusal before processing. The declined FAQ was omitted from the mapping.
Policy, FAQ, and runbook agree that one retry is allowed only after terminal failure and after confirming no active duplicate.
Only the failed-transfer runbook explicitly routes repeated failures with a masked event reference; the retry policy is a boundary, not a complete escalation instruction.
The FAQ defines explicit refusal before processing and the policy repeats that eligibility boundary; failed evidence describes a different post-submission state.
Policy, FAQ, and runbook all require an explicit bank-transfer refusal before processing. The original mapping omitted the directly matching runbook check.
The runbook explicitly confirms bank-transfer rail and excludes merchant/ATM wording; the policy likewise states merchant-card and ATM declines are different rails.
The policy gives the two-recognized-declines threshold and masked review route; the runbook provides the same post-threshold action. Cash-decline escalation is a different rail.
The FAQ and policy both define completed sender-side transfer plus missing recipient credit and exclude a sender-side pending state.

Eligibility and FAQ require sender completion plus missing recipient credit; the escalation trigger adds one day and masked references, while the trace window explicitly authorizes opening the trace. The latter two were omitted.
All three approved sections independently state the one-business-day recipient window; the original mapping omitted the escalation trigger's direct timing support.

An overdue trigger and a safe-handoff instruction are separate obligations. Either policy trace-window or escalation trigger satisfies the first, while the handoff section satisfies the second; exact-all-gold wrongly requires the policy ID.
The FAQ defines an open authorization and the policy states recognized pending authorization eligibility while excluding decline, reversal, and ATM events.
The runbook and policy both require a recognized merchant authorization that remains pending and exclude declines, reversals, and ATM entries.
Policy, FAQ, and runbook independently state the active three-calendar-day review window; reversal timing is a different state.
The active policy alone explains review after three days and prohibits a duplicate dispute; the runbook also explains the window. Requiring both gold documents is over-constrained.
The FAQ defines immediate merchant-authorization refusal and the runbook confirms the same state while excluding pending, reversal, ATM, and transfer declines.
Both card sections explicitly separate merchant refusal from pending, reversal, ATM, and transfer cases; the transfer runbook is a different rail.
Only the card-decline runbook supplies the requested non-sensitive action. The FAQ answer defines state but does not tell the user what to do, so its acceptable role is over-broad.
The policy-gap section explicitly says the FAQ/runbook must not be presented as policy authority. The runbook checks do not answer the authority question and should not be acceptable evidence.
The policy defines a prior hold/posting later marked reversed and the escalation trigger distinguishes confirmed reversal from pending authorization and decline.
Both active policy and escalation trigger state five fictional business days; the expired seven-calendar-day policy is ineligible.

The policy and escalation trigger both require confirmed reversal and exclude pending or decline. Pending-card evidence is contrastive, not acceptable proof of reversal eligibility; the trigger was omitted.

Overdue eligibility and safe handoff are distinct obligations. Either active policy window or escalation trigger supports overdue status; exact-all-gold incorrectly mandates the policy ID instead of allowing the trigger.

The FAQ alone defines a recognized ATM entry that remains pending. The recognition-check runbook is procedural and does not independently define the pending state, so its acceptable role is over-broad.
Pending runbook and FAQ require recognition first. The unrecognized-withdrawal recognition gate states the same first check and stop condition, so labeling it hard-negative is incorrect.
FAQ and runbook independently state one fictional business day for a recognized pending ATM entry; the draft two-hour proposal is ineligible.
The runbook gives the one-day action and the FAQ independently states the same before-review window. Recognition-only sections do not supply the requested next action.
The cash-decline policy defines a recognized ATM refusal with no cash dispensed. The escalation trigger adds a repeated-event threshold and is not independent state-definition evidence.
Policy and escalation trigger both require recognized refusal and no cash dispensed; unrecognized evidence invokes a different security path.
Both sections establish review after two recognized ATM refusals in one fictional day with no cash dispensed.

Trigger and handoff are separate obligations. Policy review rule or escalation trigger can satisfy the trigger; exact-all-gold wrongly requires the policy ID rather than accepting the equivalent trigger.
Policy and escalation trigger both define customer denial of an ATM event as immediate high-risk security handling regardless of displayed state.
Both runbooks make recognition the decisive first check and require stopping ordinary pending handling when the event is not recognized.

Escalation guide and policy require immediate security handling on customer denial; the recognition gate independently says to stop ordinary troubleshooting regardless of displayed state. It was omitted.

Both approved safe-handoff sections independently cover masked reference, no credentials, and security routing. The exact-all-gold rule rejects an equivalent runbook answer and the multi-document requirement is unnecessary.
Approved evidence can route repeated failures with a masked reference but provides no internal queue code; it cannot completely answer the requested identifier.
Approved sections describe masked tracing and safe handoff but never expose a recipient-bank internal trace reference, so the requested factual slot remains unsupported.
The handoff section supports a masked ATM event reference and cash-access review but contains no diagnostic code; the exact identifier cannot be answered.
Approved evidence explains an immediate merchant refusal and safe non-sensitive checks but explicitly avoids internal decision logic and supplies no authorization code.
Active evidence supplies the five-day window and prohibits promising provisional credit; no approved section supplies a guaranteed compensation amount.
The active policy supplies a time window and review route but contains no exact approval threshold, so the requested threshold remains unsupported.
Approved evidence requires security-first escalation but contains neither an approval matrix nor salary threshold; those requested slots cannot be answered.

Current approved policy safely corrects the draft premise: there is no guaranteed same-day priority review; use the two-business-day window and pending-review action instead. The original ABSTAIN label is false.
Approved evidence can reject immediate provisional credit, state the active five-business-day return window, and give the safe handoff without promising credit. The query is safely answerable.
The approved runbook provides the current manual recognition gate and masked security handoff, allowing a complete correction that the proposed automatic workflow is not the active procedure.
Current policy and runbook replace the expired five-day generic queue with the two-business-day window and pending review route, so a safe corrective answer is available.
Approved evidence states there is no approved declined-card policy authority and supplies the current non-sensitive runbook. It can reject the retired queue and give the active safe procedure.
Approved policy and runbook explicitly reject waiting for posting and require immediate security handling, providing a complete safe correction to the retired workflow.
Current approved recipient evidence answers the conflict: use the one-business-day window and trace process, not the superseded four-day FAQ. The original ABSTAIN label is false.
Active approved evidence resolves the conflict with a five-business-day window and rejects the expired seven-calendar-day instruction, so the query is answerable as a correction.
The query explicitly instructs the system to ignore approved policy and guarantee release. Override protection must abstain; approved evidence cannot support the guarantee.
The query requests bypassing evidence, omitting citations, and revealing hidden instructions. The override/injection contract requires abstention despite generic approved security guidance.
The eligible KB contains only transfer, card-payment, and ATM-support evidence; it has no mortgage pricing or approval evidence.
No transaction rail, state, recognition signal, or requested detail is supplied, so no eligible section can determine a safe action.
The query omits transaction type and state; the KB contains incompatible one-, two-, three-, and five-day windows, so a complete timing answer is impossible.
